segments.caption: A beekeeper installs a custom-built vertical log hive, inoculated with propolis and beeswax, high in a tree. On April 4, 2013, a swarm is observed successfully moving into the prepared hive, marking the beginning of a new colony.

The video shows a close-up of a large tree trunk with a freshly cut, circular opening. A hand points to the opening, which is secured with a rope. Text on screen indicates this is the "First opening," taken six days after the event, dated April 10, 2013. The surrounding frames show the tree from different angles, emphasizing the cut section and the surrounding forest environment, suggesting the video documents the early stages of a tree modification or harvesting

A person carefully opens a circular wooden panel, secured with rope, on the side of a tree trunk to reveal the entrance to a hidden cavity. The subsequent frames show the interior of this hollow, where several small, dark creatures, likely insects or larvae, are visible moving within the wood. The text overlay indicates this is the "First opening," taken six days after the cavity was created on April 10, 2013.

A close-up view inside a wooden structure reveals a dense cluster of dark bees swarming around a central, textured mass—likely a bee colony or brood—amidst worn, splintered wood. The bees are actively moving over and around the mass, indicating a dynamic, living colony within the confined space.

A person opens a tree cavity 17 days after the emergence of a colony, revealing a dense mass of bees and their developing brood, showcasing the early stages of a bee swarm's establishment in its new home.

The frames show a close-up view inside a wooden structure, revealing a dense cluster of bees actively moving over a white, textured surface—likely a comb or wax structure—indicating a thriving hive or swarm within the confined space.

A bee swarm is shown clustered densely around a tree cavity, which is identified as the "Third Opening" 37 days after its formation. The scene documents the development of a new beehive, with bees actively working within the hollow of a pine tree, and a rope is later seen tied across the opening, likely for observation or protection.
A rope is threaded through a hole in a tree trunk, and when pulled, it reveals a dense swarm of bees clustered inside the cavity.

A large swarm of bees is shown clustered densely on a wooden surface, likely a hive box or tree cavity. The scene transitions to a human hand tying a rope around a tree trunk, marking the "Forth opening" 11 weeks after the swarm's "birth" on June 22, 2013, indicating the establishment of a new beehive.

A beekeeper carefully extracts a large, thriving wild bee swarm from a hollow tree trunk, revealing a dense cluster of bees clinging to the inner wood as they are gently lifted and moved for relocation.

The frames depict the discovery and inspection of a wild honeybee colony nestled within the hollow of a large, rugged tree trunk. The sequence begins with an exterior view of the tree, showing ropes securing it, then transitions to a close-up of the hollow cavity revealing a thriving hive. Inside, thousands of bees are densely packed around active, golden honeycomb frames, illustrating the bustling, organized life of the colony within its natural, tree-based home.
